## Introduction

In this report we explore a dataset of movies taken from the Internet Movie Database (IMDb). The goal of this analysis is to see if there is a relationship between movie budgets, revenues and ratings.

The analysis has three parts:

1\. We first load and describe the data,

2\. We preprocess the data

3\. We visualise it.

## The Data

We use the `dplyr` package to manipulate the data and the `ggplot2` package to create plots.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

The data is stored in the file `CleanMovies.csv`, which we load into R as a data frame called `movies`.

```{r}
movies <- read.csv("CleanMovies.csv")
head(movies)
```

The dataset contains `r nrow(movies)` films and `r ncol(movies)` variables. For each film we have its `title`, the year it was released (`release_year`), its average viewer `rating` (out of 100), its `budget` and `revenue` (in millions of US dollars), whether it is in English (`EnglishLang`), and six `TRUE`/`FALSE` columns recording whether it belongs to each of the genres Action, Comedy, Drama, Family, Horror and SciFi.

## Preprocessing

Before analysing the data we need to clean it. Some films in the dataset
have a rating of 0, which suggests that they were never rated, and some
have a budget or revenue of less than one million dollars, which are
unlikely to be reliable. These would distort our results, so we remove
them using `filter()`. We also use `mutate()` to create two new
variables: the `profit` of each film (its revenue minus its budget), and
the `decade` in which it was released.

```{r}
movies_clean <- movies |>
  filter(rating > 0, budget >= 1, revenue >= 1) |>
  mutate(
    profit = revenue - budget,
    decade = floor(release_year / 10) * 10
  )
```

This removed `r nrow(movies) - nrow(movies_clean)` films, leaving us
with `r nrow(movies_clean)` films to analyse. As a check that our new
variables make sense, here are the five most profitable films in the
dataset:

```{r}
movies_clean |>
  slice_max(profit, n = 5) |>
  select(title, release_year, budget, revenue, profit) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Avatar and Avengers: Endgame are certainly plausible entries. Notice,
though, that *Titanic* appears twice: the 1953 and 1997 films have
exactly the same budget and revenue, which suggests the dataset has
matched some remakes to the wrong film. This is a good reminder to
always sanity-check your data, but for this report we will leave it as it is.

## Visualisation

### Movie ratings

We begin by looking at how the ratings of the movies are distributed.

```{r}
ggplot(movies_clean, aes(x = rating)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of movies ratings",
    x = "Rating (out of 100)",
    y = "Number of movies"
  )
```

Most movies have a rating between 55 and 75, with a few more poorly
rated movies forming a tail towards the lower end of the scale.
